title: Forecasting Market Risk from Scratch: Revising GARCH into an Asymmetric, Heavy-Tailed Model for Value-at-Risk
status: Draft 1 submitted (title, abstract, keywords, references). The sections below are working drafts from our prototype and will be revised for Draft 2 and the final paper.

abstract: After a calm stretch, it is easy to assume tomorrow will be calm too. Financial markets do not behave that way: quiet periods end suddenly, turbulent days tend to cluster, and large losses happen far more often than a bell curve suggests. Banks and investors summarize this risk with Value-at-Risk, the loss they expect to exceed on only a small share of days. A model that underestimates risk in turbulent periods fails exactly when it matters most. This paper studies how to forecast daily market risk from first principles. We begin with GARCH(1,1), a standard model in which today's risk depends on yesterday's surprise and yesterday's risk. We then revise two of its assumptions: that good and bad news affect risk equally, and that returns follow a normal distribution. Both models, including the maximum-likelihood fitting, will be derived and implemented from scratch in NumPy. We will estimate them on historical daily US stock market returns, forecast risk on a later period the models have not seen, and compare them using standard Value-at-Risk backtests. The goal is to explain, in plain terms, why a volatility model works, where it breaks, and how a targeted revision improves it.
keywords: Volatility Forecasting, GARCH, GJR-GARCH, Value-at-Risk, Maximum Likelihood Estimation, Backtesting

sections.title: Introduction
slides: After a calm year, the past year's volatility makes tomorrow look calm too
Risk managers set daily loss limits (Value-at-Risk) from forecasts of volatility
We derive GARCH from scratch, find where it breaks on real data, and revise it

blocks.text: At the start of February 2020, the US stock market was coming off a calm year: in 2019 its daily returns had an annualized volatility of about 13%, well below the long-run average of 18%. A risk manager who judged tomorrow by the past year would have set a 1% daily loss limit of about 1.8%. Over the next three months the market fell by more than 3% on 13 separate days, and on March 16 it fell 12%.

This is a familiar pattern in financial markets. Quiet stretches end suddenly, turbulent days cluster together, and very large losses happen far more often than a bell curve predicts. Banks, asset managers and regulators summarize this risk with Value-at-Risk (VaR): a loss threshold that should be exceeded on only a small, known share of days. A VaR model that underestimates risk in turbulent periods fails exactly when it matters most.

blocks.title: Daily US market returns and 1% Value-at-Risk limits, October 2019 to December 2020
blocks.caption: Gray bars are daily returns. Lines are the 1% VaR limits from a naive past-year rule (gray), the original GARCH model (blue) and the revised GJR-GARCH-t model (orange). Triangles mark days whose loss broke a limit.

blocks.text: This paper studies how to forecast daily market risk from first principles. We start from GARCH(1,1) (Bollerslev, 1986), which lets tomorrow's volatility depend on today's surprise and today's volatility. We derive its likelihood and implement the full fitting procedure, including the optimizer, in NumPy (Harris et al., 2020). We then examine where its assumptions conflict with real data and revise exactly those assumptions, producing an asymmetric, heavy-tailed GJR-GARCH model (Glosten et al., 1993) with Student-t errors (Bollerslev, 1987).

Both models are fitted on daily US market returns from 1990 to 2014 and evaluated on 2015 to August 2026, a period they never saw. We judge them with standard VaR backtests (Kupiec, 1995; Christoffersen, 1998) and with out-of-sample log-likelihood, against two simple benchmarks.
The paper makes three contributions:

items: A complete, transparent from-scratch implementation of GARCH estimation and VaR backtesting using only NumPy.
A controlled comparison of the original and revised models that isolates the effect of each revision on real data, including the 2020 COVID crash.
A plain-language account of why each revision helps, aimed at learners meeting volatility models for the first time.

blocks.text: Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 states the problem and derives the baseline model. Section 4 lists its assumptions. Section 5 describes the data and baseline results. Section 6 derives the revised model, Section 7 compares the models, and Sections 8 and 9 discuss limitations and lessons learned.

sections.title: Background and Related Work
slides: Returns: direction unpredictable, size predictable (Cont, 2001)
ARCH (Engle, 1982) → GARCH (Bollerslev, 1986) → GJR asymmetry (Glosten et al., 1993)
VaR backtests: right number of breaches (Kupiec) and no clustering (Christoffersen)

blocks.text: What Stock Returns Look Like

Cont (2001) summarizes patterns that appear in almost every financial market. Daily returns are nearly uncorrelated from one day to the next, so their direction is hard to predict. Their size is not: large moves cluster together (volatility clustering), extreme moves are much more common than under a normal distribution (heavy tails), and falling markets tend to become more volatile than rising ones (asymmetry, often called the leverage effect). Any useful risk model has to respect these facts.
ARCH and GARCH

Engle (1982) introduced the ARCH model, in which the variance of today's return depends on recent squared surprises. Bollerslev (1986) generalized it to GARCH by adding yesterday's variance to the equation, so a single extra term captures the slow fading of volatility that ARCH needs many lags to describe. GARCH(1,1) remains the standard starting point for volatility forecasting.
Asymmetry and Heavy Tails

Glosten, Jagannathan and Runkle (1993) added a term that raises volatility more after negative returns than after positive ones, and found the effect clearly in US stock returns. Bollerslev (1987) replaced the normal distribution of GARCH shocks with a Student-t distribution, which gives extreme days realistic weight with one extra parameter.
Value-at-Risk and Backtesting

A VaR forecast can be checked against what happened. Kupiec (1995) tests whether the share of days on which losses exceeded VaR matches the target. Christoffersen (1998) adds a test of whether those breaches arrive independently, since breaches that bunch together mean the model is slow to react when risk rises.
Does Anything Beat GARCH(1,1)?

Hansen and Lunde (2005) compared 330 volatility models. For exchange rates they found no evidence that GARCH(1,1) was beaten, but for stock returns it was clearly inferior to models that allow a leverage effect. That finding motivates the specific revision we test.

sections.title: Problem & Baseline Model
slides: Forecast tomorrow's volatility σₜ using only data up to today
GARCH(1,1): σ²ₜ = ω + α e²ₜ₋₁ + β σ²ₜ₋₁
Fitted by maximum likelihood with our own Nelder–Mead optimizer

blocks.text: Problem Statement

Each trading day, we want a forecast of how large tomorrow's market move is likely to be, using only information available today, and we want to turn that forecast into a 1% and a 5% daily Value-at-Risk.
Return Model
We write the daily return in percent as an average plus a surprise, and the surprise as volatility times a standard shock with mean 0 and variance 1:

blocks.latex: r_t = \mu + e_t, \qquad e_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} N(0, 1)
blocks.text: rₜ = μ + eₜ,   eₜ = σₜ zₜ,   zₜ ~ iid N(0, 1)
GARCH(1,1)
Tomorrow's variance is a small baseline ω, plus a reaction α to today's squared surprise, plus a share β of today's variance:
σ²ₜ = ω + α e²ₜ₋₁ + β σ²ₜ₋₁
The sum α + β, called persistence, controls how slowly a shock to volatility fades. When it is below 1, volatility drifts back to a long-run level, and half of any shock is gone after h days:
σ̄² = ω / (1 − α − β),   h = ln 0.5 / ln(α + β)
Maximum Likelihood

Volatility is never observed, so the model cannot be fitted by least squares. Instead we choose the parameters that make the observed returns most probable. With normal shocks, the negative log-likelihood is
−ℓ(ω, α, β) = ½ Σₜ [ln 2π + ln σ²ₜ + e²ₜ / σ²ₜ]
Fitting From Scratch

We minimize the negative log-likelihood with our own implementation of the Nelder–Mead simplex method (Nelder & Mead, 1965), which needs no derivatives. To keep every trial point valid, the optimizer searches over unrestricted numbers z that are mapped to parameters satisfying the constraints ω > 0, α, β ≥ 0 and α + β < 1:
ω = exp(z₀),   [α, β] = [exp(z₁), exp(z₂)] / (1 + exp(z₁) + exp(z₂))
The search is restarted from its best point with a smaller simplex until the likelihood stops improving. A test on 8,000 simulated days confirms that the procedure recovers known parameters.

blocks.text: Applications

Volatility forecasts are used to set daily loss limits and capital through Value-at-Risk, to size positions so that a portfolio holds less when risk is high, and to price options, whose value depends directly on expected volatility. In each case, underestimating risk during turbulent periods is the costly mistake.

sections.title: Data & Baseline Results
slides: Kenneth R. French Data Library: 9,233 trading days, 1990–2026
Fit on 1990–2014, test on 2015–Aug 2026 (never seen)
Baseline 1% VaR breached 60 times vs ≈29 expected

blocks.text: Data

We use the daily US stock market return from the Kenneth R. French Data Library (French, 2026): the value-weighted return of all US-listed stocks on the NYSE, AMEX and NASDAQ, built as the published excess return plus the risk-free rate, in percent. The sample runs from 1990-01-02 to 2026-08-31. We fit every model on 1990-01-02 to 2014-12-31 (6,301 days) and evaluate on 2015-01-02 to 2026-08-31 (2,932 days). Each forecast uses only returns up to the previous day, and parameters are never updated during the test period.

blocks.title: Summary statistics of daily US market returns (percent)
blocks.caption: Kurtosis is 3 for a normal distribution, where only 0.006% of days fall beyond 4 standard deviations.

blocks.text: Baseline Results

The fitted baseline has ω = 0.0123, α = 0.084 and β = 0.906. Persistence is 0.990, so half of a volatility shock fades in about 67 trading days, and the long-run daily volatility is 1.10%. These values are typical for daily stock returns.

Out of sample, the baseline's 1% VaR was breached on 60 of 2,932 days (2.05%), about twice the 29 expected, including 6 breaches during February–April 2020. That is better than the naive past-year rule (76 breaches, 12 in the crash) but still clearly too many. The table in Section 4 points to the two assumptions responsible.

sections.title: Revised Model Formulation
slides: Asymmetry: γ adds extra risk only after a bad day
Heavy tails: standardized Student-t shocks with ν degrees of freedom
Set γ = 0 and ν → ∞ and the original model comes back

blocks.text: Revision 1: Bad News Counts More
Following Glosten et al. (1993), we add a term γ that switches on only after a negative surprise:
σ²ₜ = ω + (α + γ·1[eₜ₋₁ < 0]) e²ₜ₋₁ + β σ²ₜ₋₁
Because bad days happen about half the time, persistence becomes α + γ/2 + β, and the constraints become ω > 0, α, γ, β ≥ 0 and α + γ/2 + β < 1.
Revision 2: Heavy-Tailed Shocks
Following Bollerslev (1987), the standard shock z follows a Student-t distribution with ν degrees of freedom, rescaled to variance 1 so that σ keeps its meaning. Each day contributes
ℓₜ = ln Γ((ν+1)/2) − ln Γ(ν/2) − ½ ln(π(ν−2)) − ½ ln σ²ₜ   − ((ν+1)/2) ln(1 + e²ₜ / (σ²ₜ(ν−2)))

to the log-likelihood. We require ν > 2 so the variance exists, mapping ν = 2 + exp(z) in the optimizer. The VaR quantile of the standardized t has no closed form in NumPy, so we compute its distribution function by numerical integration after substituting x = tan θ, then invert it.
A Strict Extension

Setting γ = 0 and letting ν grow without bound returns the original model, so any improvement comes from the two relaxed assumptions alone. To measure each revision separately, we also fit the two in-between models: GARCH with Student-t shocks and GJR-GARCH with normal shocks.

sections.title: Results & Comparison
slides: Revised model: α ≈ 0.001, γ ≈ 0.141: fear is louder than greed
1% VaR breaches: 60 → 51; COVID crash: 6 → 2
Best out-of-sample log score: 1.337 → 1.287

blocks.text: Fitted Models

blocks.title: Parameters fitted on 1990–2014
blocks.caption: Lower AIC and BIC are better. Half-life is in trading days. ν = ∞ denotes normal shocks.

blocks.text: Each revision lowers AIC on its own, and together they lower it by 388. Once γ is allowed, α falls almost to zero (α = 0.001, γ = 0.141 in the revised model): in this data, good surprises barely raise tomorrow's volatility, while bad surprises raise it sharply. The fitted ν ≈ 8 confirms that shocks have heavier tails than a normal distribution.

blocks.title: Tomorrow's volatility as a function of today's surprise
blocks.caption: Starting from each model's long-run volatility. After a −3% day the revised model predicts about 1.51% volatility; after a +3% day, about 1.00%. The original model predicts 1.36% for both.

blocks.text: Value-at-Risk Backtests

blocks.title: 1% VaR backtest on the test period (2,932 days; about 29 breaches expected)
blocks.caption: p-values below 0.05 reject the model. Average VaR is the mean daily loss limit in percent.

blocks.title: 5% VaR backtest on the test period (about 147 breaches expected)
blocks.caption: p-values below 0.05 reject the model.

blocks.text: At 1%, every model breaches too often and all are rejected, but the revised model comes closest (51 breaches vs 60 for the original) and was caught out on only 2 days during the COVID crash. At 5%, both GARCH models pass both tests. The rolling rule has the most cautious average limit at 1% yet the most breaches, because its caution arrives at the wrong time: it adapts too slowly going into a crisis and stays cautious long after.
Out-of-Sample Fit

blocks.title: Average negative log-likelihood per test day
blocks.caption: Lower is better. This scores the whole forecast distribution on every day, not just the tail.

blocks.text: The ranking matches the training-sample AIC: each revision helps on its own, the two combine, and the revised model forecasts unseen data best of all six.

sections.title: Discussion & Future Work
slides: The revision narrows the 1% gap but does not close it
Frozen 2014 parameters, a wilder test period, and remaining tail and skew
Next: rolling re-estimation, skewed-t, Expected Shortfall, significance tests

blocks.text: What the Revision Fixed

Both relaxed assumptions matter. Letting bad news count more makes the model react faster when markets start falling, which is when VaR breaches cluster. Heavy-tailed shocks widen the 1% limit by about 8% for the same volatility (quantile −2.51 instead of −2.33). Together they cut 1% breaches during the 2020 crash from six to two.
Why the 1% Level Still Fails

items: Parameters were estimated once, on data ending in 2014, and never updated.
The test period was more extreme than training (kurtosis 16.7 vs 11.3).
Even the fitted Student-t (ν ≈ 8) allows about 0.17% of days beyond 4 standard deviations, against 0.6% observed.
Returns are negatively skewed (-0.40 in the test period), while the Student-t is symmetric.

blocks.text: Limitations
We study one market. We have not yet tested whether the out-of-sample log-score improvement is statistically significant. VaR also says nothing about how large losses are once the limit is crossed.
Future Work

items: Re-estimate the parameters on a rolling window during the test period.
Replace the Student-t with a skewed distribution.
Add Expected Shortfall, the average loss beyond VaR.
Test the log-score difference formally and repeat the study on the 12 French industry portfolios.

sections.title: Lessons Learned
slides: Direction is unpredictable; size is predictable
A calm year makes you underestimate tomorrow
Revise the assumption that broke, then measure each fix

items: Look at the data before choosing a model: the autocorrelation of squared returns and the kurtosis told us which assumptions would fail.
When the quantity of interest is never observed, likelihood is the tool; writing the optimizer ourselves made every constraint and starting value an explicit decision.
Revise one assumption at a time and fit the in-between models, so each fix has to earn its place.
Judge forecasts on data the model has not seen, and report failures honestly: every model failed the 1% test, and that result points to the next revision.

appendix.text: The repository contains the NumPy models and tests (model/), the data downloader (tools/fetch_french.py) and data (data/), the experiment runner (model/run_garch.py), the GitHub Pages portal (index.html, style.css, script.js), the slide deck (presentations/), and local builders for the Word and PowerPoint versions (tools/). To reproduce all results and documents locally, run: make test && make garch && python3 tools/build_docx.py --stage 3 && python3 tools/build_pptx.py
